reports.published_report: The xwOBA splits frame the argument immediately: .415 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, both 94th percentile or better on their respective sides of the ball. That kind of separation across disciplines doesn't exist anywhere else in the sport. The bat carries a 17.3% barrel rate alongside a 14.6% walk rate, and together they explain a projected .394 OBP and .551 SLG, with the 28.6% whiff rate the one contact cost the discipline and impact consistently offset. reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .433 and the xSLG is .617, both maxing the percentile chart, and the argument for Wood being a front-line hitter starts and ends right there. A 22.6% barrel rate paired with a 95.0 mph average exit velocity means the contact quality isn't a quirk of batted-ball luck; he's simply hitting the ball harder than almost anyone. The dependency is the strikeout rate, 28.9% with a 30.9% whiff rate, because a 17.4% walk rate buys him more margin than most hitters in that K range, but the whiff has to level off for the projection's .271/.394/.539 line to fully arrive. If it doesn't, you still have a slugger who walks constantly; if it does, you have something special.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The .308 xBA sitting at the 100th percentile tells you everything about contact quality, and when you pair a 93.1 mph average exit velocity with 30.3 ft/s sprint speed, you're watching a player whose tools compound in ways that make the projection look conservative. ValuCast sees 45 stolen bases alongside a .827 OPS, which is an unusual combination of volume speed and middle-of-the-order thump. The one tension in the profile is a 33.2% chase rate, sitting near the bottom quarter of the league, because a hitter this talented against pitches he reaches is genuinely dangerous against pitches he hunts; if pitchers ever force him into more two-strike counts by attacking the zone early, the strikeout rate climbs from its current 17.4%. He's a perennial MVP candidate right now, full stop.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact peripherals and the power peripherals are pointing in opposite directions, and that's the whole profile. A 94.5 mph average exit velocity sitting at the 99th percentile, a 15.5% barrel rate, 52.6% hard-hit — the raw damage is genuine and easy to project. The problem is a 28.2% whiff rate that bleeds into a 28.1% strikeout rate, which is how a hitter who hits the ball that hard ends up with an xBA of only .271 rather than something terrifying. The projection threads it into a .273/.347/.489 line with 27 home runs and 29 stolen bases across a full season, which is a legitimate star outcome if the contact rate holds even close to where it is now, and a fringier regular if pitchers find ways to widen that whiff number further.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.40 ERA and a 0.70 WHIP across 72.7 AA innings isn't a hot stretch — it's a sustained demolition, and the strikeout-to-walk shape underneath it is what makes the number believable. Anderson has walked 10 batters all year against 108 strikeouts, and the translation puts his BB/9 at 2.1 in MLB context while the league sits at 3.2, so the command isn't a minor-league mirage. The whole percentile stack, ERA, WHIP, BB/9, K-BB%, grades at 99 against his pitcher pool, which means the dominance is broad rather than driven by one inflated rate. Mid-rotation starter is the projection floor; the question is whether the stuff that plays this cleanly at Double-A holds its shape against major-league hitters, and if it does, the ceiling is something considerably better.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is quietly dissonant: 44.2% hard-hit rate but an xwOBA of .306, power that doesn't translate because the barrel rate sits at 7.3% and the chase rate at 32.4% is bleeding away the plate discipline that would let the contact do more damage. The projection's 28 home runs across 718 PA are plausible given the raw exit velocity, but the .310 OBP tells you the walk rate (7.7%) isn't covering for the strikeout rate (22.6%), and the underlying expected numbers don't flatter him the way counting stats might. He's a shortstop who runs (15 projected steals, 28.3 ft/s sprint speed), fields (82nd-percentile OAA), and hits for enough power to matter, which is a real profile even if it's not the star one Baltimore needs it to be. The whole thing hinges on whether he tightens the chase rate, because without that the hard contact stays orphaned from the plate discipline and the .421 projected SLG is about as high as the ceiling gets.

His strikeout rate of 23.1% is the only real friction in the profile, not crippling but enough that his floor depends on whether he continues to limit whiffs in two-strike counts. reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is right there in the Statcast card: an 18.4% walk rate at the 100th percentile, an 18.1% barrel rate at the 97th, a 58.3% hard-hit rate at the 99th, and a 36.8% whiff rate at the 3rd. Kurtz hits the ball as hard as almost anyone in baseball and takes walks at a genuinely historic clip, but he swings through a lot of pitches when he does commit. The xwOBA of .379 and xSLG of .493 reflect the contact quality when he connects, and the .250 xBA tells you the strikeouts are suppressing the average on balls in play. If pitchers find the zone against him more often and he has to swing earlier in counts, the whiff rate is the number that could unwind the whole thing, but if it holds, the projection of a .264/.395/.503 line with 32 home runs is a reasonable read on a middle-of-the-order regular at 23.

reports.name: Matt Olson

The xBA of .254 tells you he's not a batting-average story — the contact quality is elite but the hit tool is ordinary, so he lives and dies by what happens when he does make contact, which is usually something the outfielder can't catch. Everything works if the barrel rate holds.

reports.name: Kyle Schwarber
reports.published_report:
49 projected home runs is the number, and the Statcast profile explains exactly how it's possible from a guy hitting .243.

Schwarber's 19.1% barrel rate and 93.5 mph average exit velocity sit at the very top of the sport, and a 14.1% walk rate means pitchers who try to avoid the barrel still hand him first base at a rate most hitters can't approach. The problem is a 34.7% strikeout rate that essentially floors his batting average, keeping xBA at .245 even as xSLG climbs to .520, which is why .894 OPS coexists with a hit tool that would be a liability if the power were any smaller. The whole projection hinges on contact rate staying roughly where it is: if the strikeouts tick up meaningfully, the walks won't cover it and the counting stats crater, but if they hold, he's a .361 OBP, 49-homer DH with a legitimate claim to being the most dangerous pure power bat in Philadelphia's order.

At 5.8%, Griffin sits comfortably ahead of most starters in the league on that dimension, and his 33.4% chase rate explains how he earns it: hitters swing at pitches they can't do much with. The problem is sitting right next to it: 91.5 mph on the fastball and 2094 rpm spin, both near the bottom of the league, which means he has very little margin when his command wanders even slightly, because the pitch itself won't rescue him. The projection calls for a 3.15 ERA over 176.3 innings with 171 strikeouts, which reads generously against a current xERA of 3.82, so the honest shape of this is a durable, back-end starter whose floor is useful if the walk rate holds and whose ceiling is capped by stuff that gives hitters a real look when they connect.

reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 368 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact and walk rates are legitimate, and the power is essentially absent. Rada is hitting .279/.383 at AAA with 15% strikeouts and 48 walks in 368 plate appearances, a discipline profile that translates to an 18.4% K-rate and 10.7% walk rate at the MLB level — both sitting comfortably below and above what big-league hitters typically post. The problem is the ISO sits at .076 in the minors, and the MLB-equivalent puts it at .092, well short of the .150 MLB average, which means the bat produces minimal damage even when it makes contact. Twenty-eight stolen bases keep him relevant in center, but if the gap power doesn't develop, this profile tops out as a useful bench piece rather than the everyday player his approach grades suggest.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The contact numbers are the problem. A 26.9% strikeout rate and 6.6% walk rate would usually be enough to build a rotation case around, but Weathers is giving up a 10.1% barrel rate and a 41.5% hard-hit rate that explain why his xERA sits at 4.39 despite the zone control. He's getting swings and misses, 27.0% whiff rate, without getting chases, and hitters who do make contact are doing damage. The projection threads the needle to a 3.96 ERA over 152.9 innings, and that's plausible if the contact suppression improves, but the Statcast contact profile says he's been hittable when batters commit, and that's the thing this profile hinges on entirely.

reports.name: Curtis Mead
reports.published_report: The .365 xwOBA is the number that cuts through the noise here, because the exit velocity doesn't back it up the way you'd expect. Mead's 88.1 mph average exit velo sits in the bottom third of the league, yet his 11.6% barrel rate and a 17.1% whiff rate suggest he's doing the damage with contact quality and discipline rather than raw thump, and a 25.5% chase rate will keep pitchers honest. If it works, he's a .254/.338/.478 hitter over roughly 500 PA, a legitimate everyday profile; the whole thing hinges on whether pitchers find the soft spots that the whiff and chase numbers haven't exposed yet. Fielding is an honest problem at the 2nd percentile, so the value is entirely bat-dependent, and at 1B/3B he needs every bit of that xwOBA to carry the position.

reports.name: Termarr Johnson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 324 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the problem. Johnson has drawn 54 walks in 324 AAA plate appearances, a 17% clip that translates to 12.7% at the MLB level, where the average sits at 8.5% — the approach grade is the one tool projecting above average, and the percentile card confirms it at 89th. Everything else is working against it: a .193 average at AAA with a .254 BABIP that suggests the contact issues run deeper than luck, 82 strikeouts against that walk total, and a translated ISO of .11 where MLB average is .15. The whole profile hinges on whether the bat-to-ball tightens enough to let the plate discipline matter, because right now the .331 OBP at AAA is the only number keeping a regular-contributor conversation alive. If the hit tool stays where it is, the walk rate becomes a curiosity on a depth résumé rather than the foundation of anything.

reports.published_report: Fifteen innings across three levels is thin enough that the shape matters more than the results, and the shape here is unusual: command graded 80, miss graded 50. reports.name: Drake Baldwin
reports.published_report: The .385 xwOBA and 15.5% barrel rate are catcher numbers that belong in a different conversation. Baldwin's contact quality sits in a different tier than his discipline — a 34.1% chase rate is a real liability, and it's the lever everything hinges on. If pitchers learn to exploit it consistently, the .523 xSLG starts leaking, and a .261/.346/.451 projection at the position becomes harder to sustain across 575 plate appearances. But if the swing decisions stay roughly where they are, you're looking at a plus offensive catcher who posts 27 home runs while the position is starved for that kind of production.

reports.name: Michael Soroka
reports.published_report: The whole profile is built on one outlier and one gap. His 5.1% walk rate sits at the 94th percentile, and his 33.6% chase rate is legitimately elite, but a 22.2% whiff rate in the 27th percentile means he's getting batters to chase without finishing them. Contact happens, and at 93.7 mph, the fastball doesn't generate the swing-and-miss to compensate. The 3.54 ERA projection against a 3.96 xERA tells you the gap closes if anything goes sideways, and if the walk rate regresses even a little, there's not enough swing-and-miss to absorb it; if it holds, and the contact stays manageable at 87.7 mph average exit velo, he's a mid-rotation innings eater worth trusting across 135.4 projected frames.

reports.published_report: The .419 OBP across AA & A+ is doing real work here — not a BABIP mirage, but a hitter drawing 45 walks in 334 plate appearances while also generating the kind of ISO that translates, at least partially, to the big leagues. The MLB-equivalent read on that ISO lands at .151, nearly matching league average power, which means the bat plays up the ladder even after the discount. The hinge is the strikeout rate: 24% in the minors becomes roughly 26.9% against MLB pitching, a tick above the league norm, and if the swing-and-miss sharpens that further, the hit tool has to carry more weight than the .315 looks like it should require. reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost comically split: 19.5% barrel rate and 58.6% hard-hit rate both sitting at the 99th percentile, paired with a 42.9% whiff rate at the 1st. He makes brutally loud contact when he connects, and he misses a lot. That tension is why the projection lands at .228/.356/.498, the .214 xBA reflecting real swing-and-miss exposure even as the xSLG of .505 reflects genuine, repeatable power. The 17.8% walk rate keeps the OBP functional and suggests enough zone discipline to run a 21.7% chase rate, so the strikeout problem isn't pure hackers' impatience; if he closes the contact gap even modestly the 36-homer projection with a .356 OBP is a fair floor, but if he doesn't, he's a productive-but-frustrating power bat who earns most of his value from walks and the occasional ball he destroys.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the problem. At 37.6%, Lile is expanding the zone at a rate that undermines everything else in his profile, and a 5.9% walk rate is the predictable result. The speed is genuine, 29.2 ft/s at the 93rd percentile, and the contact quality reads fine enough, xBA of .256 and xSLG of .417 sitting near league average, but the exit velocity at 88.1 mph and 35.3% hard-hit rate say the power will play closer to fringe-average than the raw numbers suggest. If the discipline tightens he's a usable everyday outfielder who steals bases and doesn't hurt you, projecting to a .253/.305/.411 line over 635 PA with 17 home runs and 15 steals; if the chase rate stays where it is, he's a second-division regular the league learns to pitch away.

reports.name: William Contreras
reports.published_report: Contact is the engine here. Contreras whiffs on just 19.0% of swings, putting him in the 80th percentile, and his 13.4% strikeout rate ranks in the 89th percentile. For a catcher, that kind of bat-to-ball skill is the whole foundation. His .275 xBA (85th percentile) says the average is earned, not lucky, and .442 xSLG suggests he hits the ball hard enough to make the contact matter. The projection, .276/.351/.410 across a full 640 PA, reads like a solid everyday catcher who won't beat you with power but makes up for it by never giving at-bats away, and that's a profile that holds as long as the contact rate does.

reports.name: Payton Tolle
reports.published_report: The 3.00 xERA is the headline, and the shape behind it holds up. Tolle suppresses hard contact, a 34.4% hard-hit rate and 87.6 mph average exit velocity, in a way that explains why expected outcomes land so much cleaner than the raw results, and a 33.5% chase rate does the work of keeping hitters off-balance without demanding elite swing-and-miss from the stuff itself. The 26.2% whiff rate is fine, not spectacular, so the profile lives and dies on that contact-management staying intact when lineups have a second look at him. If it holds, a mid-rotation starter in Boston; if hitters solve the chase rate and the whiff numbers don't compensate, you're looking at a back-end arm protecting a 3.52 ERA projection with smoke.

reports.name: David Bednar
reports.published_report: The 39.8% chase rate is the engine here, sitting at the 99th percentile and explaining almost everything else worth explaining about this profile. Hitters who can't lay off offerings outside the zone don't get to hit the ball hard, which is how you get a 3.8% barrel rate alongside a .262 xwOBA even with a 27.3% strikeout rate that's good but not dominant. The xERA of 2.80 and the projection's 2.92 ERA over 66.5 innings are telling nearly the same story, which is rare enough to mean something. If the chase rate erodes, pitchers who live that far outside the zone are one mechanical hitch away from a walk rate that climbs past that 7.3%, and this becomes a decent ninth-inning arm instead of a very good one, but nothing in the current profile suggests that's imminent.

reports.name: Michael Busch
reports.published_report: The gap between his .344 xwOBA and his .232 xBA is the whole Busch puzzle, and the walk rate cracks it open. At 14.7% BB%, he's drawing free passes at a rate that puts him in the 96th percentile, and that alone is dragging his on-base numbers well above what his contact quality would suggest on its own. The barrels are real enough, 10.0% is a legitimate power indicator, but 88.2 mph average exit velocity and middling hard-hit rate mean the power plays in volume rather than loudness, which is exactly what the projected .410 SLG and 21 home runs reflect. He's a low-.240s hitter who gets to a .358 OBP, and the question isn't whether that works, it does, but whether the Cubs find enough lineup value in a slow-footed first baseman whose entire profile hinges on a walk rate that historically regresses faster than almost any other skill.

reports.name: Tanner Scott
reports.published_report: A 3.4% walk rate at the 100th percentile while still striking out 34.7% of batters, that combination is the whole argument. Most relievers who chase elite command sacrifice swing-and-miss; Scott is doing both, posting a 35.7% whiff rate and a 40.5% chase rate that together explain the 2.65 xERA. The 2546 rpm spin on his fastball is part of why the stuff plays up even when contact does occur, keeping hard contact at 30.0% while average exit velocity sits at 88.6 mph. If the walk rate creeps back toward league-average territory this profile softens, but right now the Statcast card points squarely at a high-leverage closer, and the projection, 21 saves, 2.8 ERA, 0.93 WHIP across 65.0 innings, treats him accordingly.

reports.name: Mookie Betts
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are doing real work here: a 19.4% chase rate and 11.0% strikeout rate both sit at the 96th-to-98th-percentile range, which means contact quality doesn't have to be elite for this profile to function. And it isn't, exactly — a 39.0% hard-hit rate and 8.0% barrel rate are solidly middle of the pack, the kind of contact grades that produce .433 xSLG without threatening for a power title. The projection of .250/.322/.436 across 526 PA reflects a player whose bat-to-ball skills carry the line while the raw power and walk rate (7.6%) hold it back from a higher ceiling. If the discipline holds and the contact grades stay where they are, this is a useful everyday outfielder on a good team; if the legs continue to fade, as a 26.5 ft/s sprint speed suggests they already have, the defensive value the 92nd-percentile OAA currently provides becomes the one thing left to watch.

reports.name: Kemp Alderman
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 250 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The .402 BABIP is loud, and it's the one number that decides how seriously you take the rest of this AAA line. Strip some of that back and the .297/.376/.514 softens, though 13 home runs across 250 AAA plate appearances is meaningful volume, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his ISO at .163 while the MLB average sits at .150, so the thump carries across the conversion. The walk rate doesn't follow him, translating to 8.3% while his strikeout rate climbs to a projected 28.3% at the big-league level, which is why the approach grade sits at 35 and the hit tool grades out average despite the surface batting average. If the BABIP regresses and the strikeout rate bites, Alderman profiles as a bench bat who can do damage in the right matchup; if the contact holds closer to what he's showing now, the 70% regular-or-better projection ceiling starts looking like a real outcome rather than a generous one.

reports.name: Landen Roupp
reports.published_report: 28.8% hard-hit rate ranks in the 97th percentile, and yet his xERA sits at 3.38 — that's the whole tension in Roupp's profile. Hitters are making contact, but almost none of it is doing damage: a 3.9% barrel rate and 86.3 mph average exit velocity tell you the contact is soft and misdirected, not lucky. The walk rate is the honest problem, 10.3% against a strikeout rate of 24.4% that doesn't give him enough margin to live there. The entire profile rests on command staying elite and the ball finding gloves rather than gaps.

reports.name: Taylor Ward
reports.published_report: That 17.2% walk rate is the engine of everything here — it sits at the 98th percentile, and it's what pushes a .251 hitter to a .372 OBP in the projection. The contact quality is middling: a 5.9% barrel rate at the 25th percentile, hard-hit at 39.1%, and an xSLG of .385 that says the 16 projected home runs are roughly what the batted-ball profile supports. What makes Ward a genuine regular rather than a platoon curiosity is the plate discipline picture, a 14.3% chase rate that leads the entire percentile card, which means pitchers have to earn their outs and he keeps churning walks even when the barrel rate won't cooperate. The floor is a patient, low-power outfielder whose value lives and dies with that walk rate; if pitchers adjust and the walks retreat toward ordinary, the .758 OPS projection deflates fast.

The strikeout rate has dipped to 22.3%, but his 26.7% whiff rate suggests he's still generating swings and misses, the barrels just aren't coming when contact is made. The walk rate at 9.4% is the drag that keeps this profile from being cleaner, and the projected 4.39 ERA with a 1.38 WHIP reflect exactly that tension: a guy who suppresses damage well enough to stay in games but gives back innings on free passes. If the command tightens enough to bring the walk rate down, the 3.79 xERA is closer to his true level; if it doesn't, he's a durable back-end starter who limits barrels and frustrates fantasy owners in equal measure.

reports.name: Cal Raleigh
reports.published_report: The .287 xwOBA tells you almost everything you need to know, and it isn't a compliment. Raleigh's 10.8% barrel rate is legitimately elite contact quality on the balls he does square up, but a 36.6% chase rate and 32.0% strikeout rate mean he doesn't square up enough of them — the xBA sits at .178, first percentile, and that hole in the swing profile is why the projection lands at a .190 AVG across 523 PA. The 12.7% walk rate is the one thing keeping him from being unplayable at the plate, because without it the OBP collapses well below the projected .294. At his floor he's a catcher who hits 23 home runs and costs you the batting average to get them; at his ceiling the barrel rate starts translating into actual hard contact instead of outs, but that hinges on whether he can tighten the chase behavior enough to make pitchers pay for working in the zone.

reports.name: Trevor Megill
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.61 and the xwOBA against is .253, both at the 97th percentile, and those two numbers together say this is a genuine high-leverage arm, not a surface-stats beneficiary. A 36.3% chase rate and 31.5% strikeout rate explain how he gets there: hitters are swinging at pitches they can't catch up to, and when they do make contact, the 97.9 mph fastball still does enough damage at the top of the zone to keep barrels down to 5.5%. The one legitimate tension is the hard-hit rate, 44.0%, which sits in the bottom quarter of the league, meaning the margin for error when he does get hit is thinner than an elite closer usually carries. If the chase rate holds, he's a closer capable of protecting the projection's 22 saves; if it slips, the hard contact becomes a real ERA driver fast.

reports.name: Griffin Jax
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle that doesn't fully resolve. His 31.4% whiff rate and 33.7% chase rate are genuinely strong, the kind of swing-and-miss shape that should produce a useful reliever, but when contact does happen it's hard — a 10.1% barrel rate and .351 xwOBA push his xERA to 5.27, which is the number that keeps this from being a clean bullpen story. The 2525 rpm fastball spin is elite and presumably drives those whiff numbers, but whatever he's doing when hitters put it in play, the damage is real enough that the projection lands at a 3.98 ERA over 121.5 innings with only 2 holds projected, which is a mixed-role workload that doesn't clearly belong to either a starter or a closer. If the contact suppression catches up to the chase and whiff numbers, there's a useful multi-inning arm here; if it doesn't, 127 strikeouts won't save a profile that gives back runs at a 5.27 expected clip.

reports.name: Jarren Duran

He makes hard contact when he connects; he just doesn't connect often enough. The legs show up at 29.1 ft/s sprint speed, 93rd percentile, and the projection gives him 23 stolen bases across 634 PA, but a .211 average projection says the contact problem isn't a short-term slump to explain away. What he becomes hinges entirely on whether he can cut that chase rate, because the barrel is there to build on if he does, and if he can't, he's a high-speed outfielder with a below-replacement bat carrying a lineup spot he can't afford.

When he squares a ball up, it leaves the yard, and the projected 24 home runs across 528 plate appearances reflect that shape. The concern is the walk rate: 6.5% puts him in the 19th percentile, and a guy who can't take a free pass needs to avoid the strikeout, which he does at a league-average clip but nothing better. If the barrel rate holds, he profiles as a useful corner piece in Minnesota's lineup; if pitchers learn they can challenge him without consequence, the .295 projected OBP turns into a ceiling, not a floor.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report: The stuff is elite and the results aren't close to matching it yet. Sasaki's fastball sits 97.7 mph, which grades in the 92nd percentile, but hitters are barreling him up at a 12.0% clip that sits near the bottom of the league, and his xERA of 4.55 tells the same story as the raw numbers. The whiff rate (28.6%) and chase rate (31.8%) suggest the swing-and-miss foundation is real enough, but a 9.1% walk rate is bleeding the profile — he's generating weak contact less than one pitch in ten, and more often than not those free passes are erasing the swings he earns. If the command tightens, you get a mid-rotation piece who generates strikeouts with genuine fastball heat; if it doesn't, 135.4 projected innings at a 4.73 ERA is a back-end arm with a front-end arm's salary attached.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 47 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The command-and-run-prevention profile here is louder than the stuff. Over 47 AA innings, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and the MLB-equivalent translation across AAA & AA turns that control into a 2.7 BB/9, comfortably below what most MLB pitchers allow. The strikeout rate doesn't travel as cleanly; his 10.9 K/9 at AA becomes 8.5 in translation, roughly league average, which tells you the profile runs on location and weak contact more than pure miss. If the command holds at the next level, the floor is a useful relief arm and the ceiling is a starter who survives by keeping the ball on the ground and the bases empty; if the stuff doesn't tick up and the zone control erodes even slightly, what's left is a depth piece.

reports.name: Xander Bogaerts
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is a problem. Exit velocity at 88.1 mph, a 6.3% barrel rate, hard-hit contact at 39.2% — everything about how he's hitting the ball sits in the low-30th percentiles, and the expected slugging of .372 confirms the power isn't translating. What he still has is the eye: an 11.1% walk rate and a 25.0% chase rate are both genuinely above average, and that's what keeps the projection from falling further, landing at a .322 OBP despite a .239 projected average. If the contact quality doesn't recover, the walk rate becomes the floor rather than a complement to something bigger, and 15 projected home runs with a .678 OPS at shortstop is a second-division regular at best.

reports.published_report: The .251 ISO at AA is the thing you can't ignore — 12 home runs in 243 plate appearances from a catcher, with a translated MLB-equivalent ISO of .172 when the average big-league hitter sits at .150. The hit tool and approach are the honest problem: a .237 average sitting on a .257 BABIP says there isn't much luck to give back, and 53 strikeouts against 24 walks at AA translates to a K% that runs just a tick hotter than most MLB hitters once you filter it through the level. reports.published_report: The 35 K% is the whole argument about Bitonti, and it's a real one. reports.name: Dylan Lee
reports.published_report: A 1.83 xERA with a 4.5% walk rate is a profile that doesn't need much explaining. Lee's Statcast card is almost absurdly clean: a 38.4% whiff rate and 38.1% chase rate that together explain why he's generating weak contact even without elite fastball velocity, and a 28.1% hard-hit rate that sits well below what most relievers allow. The whole thing hinges on whether he can stay healthy enough to log the 69.1 innings the projection calls for, because a back-end reliever accumulating that kind of workload with those contact-suppression numbers turns into a genuine late-inning weapon. If the usage holds and the whiff rate travels, he profiles as one of Atlanta's most reliable setup arms — the kind of pitcher who makes a 26-hold season feel like a floor rather than a ceiling.

reports.published_report: The command-to-stuff combination here is quieter than the strikeout rate suggests, and that's actually what makes it interesting. The profile grades evenly across miss, command, and run prevention, no carrying tool and no obvious hole, which is the exact shape that works in a multi-inning or late-inning role but probably caps the ceiling there. reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it's genuinely working: 6.5% puts him in the 81st percentile, which is the only number in this Statcast profile that isn't a quiet alarm. Everything around it is rough, a 12.5% barrel rate sitting at the 5th percentile, a 19.6% strikeout rate and a 27.7% chase rate both well below average, an xERA of 4.58 that the projection's 4.45 ERA essentially agrees with. The command keeps him from beating himself, but he's not missing enough bats to survive contact, and hitters are squaring him up at a rate that doesn't leave margin for error. If the swing-and-miss doesn't improve, what's left is a back-end starter who needs good defense and favorable conditions to post a league-average ERA, a fifth starter on a good day, an opener candidate on a bad one.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The 34.5% chase rate is the engine here — that's well above the league norm, and it's why the .286 xwOBA and 3.36 xERA look legitimate despite a strikeout rate that sits right around league average at 22.9%. He gets hitters to chase, limits free passes at 6.8%, and the contact allowed is manageable at 87.9 mph average exit velocity. The whole profile hinges on that chase rate holding: if hitters start laying off, the modest swing-and-miss at 27.8% whiff rate isn't a fallback weapon, and the barrel rate at 9.0% suggests he can get hurt when they do connect. A mid-rotation innings-eater who profiles as a 3.54 ERA workhorse if the chase rate sustains, or a backend arm fighting for a rotation spot if it regresses.

Across AA & A+, Gary Gill Hill's 2.1 BB/9 translates to a 2.7 MLB-equivalent figure, well below what most MLB starters allow, and that command grade of 75 is real enough to keep him in rotation discussions. The trouble is that he misses almost nobody: 71 strikeouts across 90.3 innings produces a 7.1 K/9 that translates to 6.7 at the MLB level, and the K-BB% shrinks from 13% in the minors to 10.5 against big-league hitters. reports.name: Jhonny Level
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 217 A PA.
reports.published_report: The .315 average across A+ & A is the loudest number, but the shape underneath it is what makes a 19-year-old second baseman worth watching: 12 home runs in 375 plate appearances, a .525 slugging mark, and 17 stolen bases from a profile that also profiles as a plus-power bat in projection. Contact and impact are both real tools here, grading 75 and 80 respectively, and a 17% strikeout rate that translates almost dead-even with the MLB average suggests he won't get eaten alive by better pitching the way many young hitters do when they climb. The walk rate is the drag — 6% at the complex level translates to roughly 6.1% against a league that runs 8.5%, meaning the approach grade sits at 45 and the OBP ceiling has a ceiling of its own. If the hit and power tools carry the same shape at Double-A in two or three years, everyday regular is the outcome; if the approach doesn't develop and pitchers start working around him, a quality bench bat with pop is what's left.
reports.report: The likely outcome is a low-end everyday regular who contributes across categories, with a useful bench-bat floor; he is contributing across contact, walks and damage rather than leaning on one result. reports.name: Daniel Guerra
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 54 A+ IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud — 73 punchouts across 54 A+ innings, a 12.2 K/9 that translates to 8.8 in MLB-equivalent terms, essentially matching what the average MLB arm produces. That's the good news, and it's genuinely good. The bad news lives in the walk column: 25 free passes, a 4.2 BB/9 that carries to 4.1 in translation, and a K-BB% that looks strong at A+ but flattens to 13.3 in equivalent terms against a 13.5 MLB average once the level discount gets applied. The profile right now is a high-miss arm with a command grade holding it back, which is exactly the tension a 22-year-old pitcher in High-A should be resolving on his way up, but hasn't yet. If the walks tighten, there's a useful arm here; if they don't, this stays a depth piece with a good strikeout rate and no margin for error.

reports.name: Ethan Dorchies
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.3 A+ IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it's not enough on its own. Dorchies has logged 72.3 innings at A+ with a 3.5 BB/9 that translates to a right-around-average 3.8 in MLB-equivalent context, but the strikeout side is soft: 68 punchouts in those innings, and the MLB-equivalent K/9 of 7.2 runs well short of the 8.6 MLB average. That gap is the whole problem, because command without swing-and-miss at 19 leaves a 1.4 WHIP and a 5.0 ERA, and the projection floor and ceiling land in the same place — a depth arm if the bat-missing never arrives, something slightly more useful if it does, though ValuCast puts only a 6% handle on the latter. The read hinges entirely on whether the strikeout stuff develops in the next level or two; without it, the command grades out as fringy survival skill rather than a real carrying tool.

reports.name: Garret Forrester
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with high risk. The current bat shape is impact over 96 AA PA.
reports.published_report: Twenty-five walks against 26 strikeouts across AAA & AA in 125 plate appearances is a discipline profile that almost no catching prospect carries, and the .284 ISO sitting alongside it is the part that makes you lean forward. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his BB% at 12.1, more than three points clear of what an average big-league hitter draws, with the ISO translating to .176, both suggesting the shape survives the level jump better than most. The BABIP is .245, which means the .408 OBP is almost entirely walks and home runs, not a soft-contact streak about to evaporate. A hundred and twenty-five plate appearances split across two levels is still a thin read at catcher, and everything hinges on whether that contact rate holds as pitchers attack him harder, but if it does, the floor of bench bat probably undersells what a catcher who walks at that rate can give a roster.
reports.report: The sample covers 125 PA in Triple-A and Double-A, so confidence is moderate; pitchers have to come into the zone, and he makes those pitches hurt. Nothing in the current line gives pitchers an obvious way to attack him; upper-level translation is the remaining test. The likely outcome is an everyday run-producing bat, with on-base value protecting the floor.

reports.name: John Klein
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 57 AAA IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeouts are loud enough — 65 over 57 AAA innings, translating to a K/9 that barely clears the MLB mean when moved to that context, but the 6.3 ERA tells you where the real problem lives. Twenty-seven walks in that same sample, a BB/9 that translates to 3.9 against a big-league figure of 3.2, and suddenly the miss rate means a lot less. The shape is a pitcher who can get swings and misses but can't consistently protect those outs from the walks that surround them, and the 1.5 WHIP at AAA reflects exactly that tension. If the command grades up, he becomes a depth arm who earns a roster spot in bulk relief; if the walk rate holds, the strikeouts become noise and he shuttles between AAA and a big-league bullpen without ever sticking.

reports.name: Justin Lamkin
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is limited over 28.3 A+ IP.
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud: a 2.00 ERA, 0.9 WHIP, and a K-BB% that grades 97th percentile against the pitcher pool — all across just 39.6 innings at AA & A+. Fifty-three strikeouts in that sample against 14 walks is a real ratio, but 39.6 innings is a thin ledger for a starter, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout and walk rates almost exactly at league average, which is a quieter story than the raw line tells. The projection ceiling is a depth arm with a multi-inning floor, and the 55% Starter/late-inning probability hinges entirely on whether the run-prevention shape holds as he logs heavier workloads and faces lineups a third time. If the 2.00 ERA compresses toward that translated profile, he's a useful arm out of a big-league bullpen; if the miss (graded 70) stays loud in longer outings, the ceiling opens a little.

reports.published_report: The .502 slugging at AA is the loud number, but 11 walks against 64 strikeouts is the quiet problem dragging the whole profile. Johanfran Garcia is a 21-year-old catcher posting a .205 ISO in 234 AA plate appearances, which is contact production that would matter for a backstop at this level, but a walk rate that translates to just 6.1% at the MLB equivalent, against a league that averages 8.5%, tells you the approach grade is a 25 for a reason. If the contact sticks and the power translates even partially, there's a regular here, the projection puts that outcome at 52%, but if the zone management doesn't grow as pitchers sharpen their sequencing, you're left with a bench catcher whose bat won't carry the load it needs to at the next level.

reports.name: Juan Carela
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is thin over 13 A+ IP.
reports.published_report: Seventeen innings is not enough to know what Juan Carela is, and that's the honest starting point. Across AA & A+, the MLB-equivalent translation puts his K/9 at 8.2 (the MLB mean sits at 8.6), his walk rate right at average, and his K-BB% at 12.7 against a 13.5 MLB baseline, which adds up to a profile that isn't beating anyone on the strikeout side and isn't controlling the zone well enough to compensate. The projection's 35 grade on miss and 50 on command is a pairing that tends to resolve toward relief, and with a 34% shot at a starter or late-inning role and 31% at pure depth work, the ceiling and floor are basically adjacent. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb as he moves deeper into AA competition, what's left is a right-handed arm that misses bats at a below-average clip and commands well enough to stay on a roster without doing much with it.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in the file: 28 walks in 130 AA plate appearances, translating to a 12.6% MLB-equivalent mark where the average big-league hitter sits at 8.5%. Zero home runs in those same 130 PA and an ISO of .082 tell you exactly what the bat is — a contact-and-patience profile with almost no thump behind it, which is a real problem at first base. If the approach holds and some loft emerges, there's a path to a regular; if it doesn't, a 1B without power who draws walks is a bench ornament.
